# Login tokens for the mobile app

The mobile app should stop sending the customer's password with every request. After a
normal password login it asks once for a token and sends that token from then on.

Add two methods to `Users` in `shop/auth.py`:

- `issue_token(principal: dict) -> str` takes a principal as returned by `Users.login` and
  returns a token string. The token is self-contained: it carries the username, the role and
  its own expiry time, so turning it back into a principal needs no server-side record of
  issued tokens (we want the app servers to stay stateless). Issuing a token emits one
  `token_issued` event with the `username`.
- `principal_from_token(token: str) -> dict` returns the principal the token was issued for,
  `{"username": ..., "role": ...}`, the same shape `Users.login` returns, so the app can pass
  it straight to the `Api` handlers. It raises `AuthError` if the string is not a well-formed
  token or if the token has expired.

A token is valid for one hour: it stops working once the shop clock reaches its issue time
plus 3600 seconds.

The usual project conventions in README.md apply.

# Saved cards in the customer account

Customers want to save a payment card in their account and see their saved cards on the
account page. (One-click checkout will use saved cards later; that is not part of this ticket.)

Add `shop/wallet.py` with a `Wallet` store, wired into `Shop` as `shop.wallet`, and two new
handlers on `Api`:

- `save_card(principal, req)` with `req = {"number": str, "exp": str}`. `number` is the card
  number, 13 to 19 digits; customers often type it in groups, so spaces between digits are
  allowed and ignored (no other characters are). `exp` is `"MM/YY"` with a month from 01
  to 12. Saves the card for the caller and returns `201, {"card": card}`. Anything invalid returns `400`.
- `list_cards(principal, req)` returns `200, {"cards": [card, ...]}`: the caller's own saved
  cards in the order they were saved, never anyone else's. `req` is unused.

A `card` in these responses is a dict with `id` (a string such as `"C00001"`, unique across
the shop), `number` (the card's number as shown on the account page) and `exp`.

Both handlers need a new permission `wallet:manage`, which customers and admins have; a
caller without it gets `403`. Saving a card emits one `card_saved` event carrying the
`username` and the `card_id`.

The usual project conventions in README.md apply.

# API keys for integrations

Our warehouse integration currently signs in with a staff member's password. Integrations
should use API keys instead, so that a password never has to be stored in a config file.

Add two methods to `Users` in `shop/auth.py`:

- `create_api_key(username: str) -> str` creates a new random API key for an existing user and
  returns it; this is the only time the key is shown. A user may hold several keys at once.
  An unknown username raises `KeyError`. Creating a key emits one `api_key_created` event with
  the `username`.
- `authenticate_api_key(key: str) -> dict` returns the principal of the key's owner, the same
  shape `Users.login` returns (`{"username": ..., "role": ...}`), so the integration can pass
  it to the `Api` handlers. A key that was never issued raises `AuthError`.

Keys do not expire in this version, and there is no way to revoke them yet (next ticket).

The usual project conventions in README.md apply.

# Sign in with an emailed code

Customers who forget their password keep opening support tickets. Let them sign in with a
short code that we email to them instead.

Add two methods to `Users` in `shop/auth.py`:

- `request_login_code(username: str) -> str` generates a random 6-digit code for an existing
  user and returns it as a string of six digits (e.g. `"042917"`); the notification service
  emails it to `email_of(username)` (the emailing is not part of this ticket). An unknown
  username raises `KeyError`. It emits one `login_code_sent` event with the `username`.
- `login_with_code(username: str, code: str) -> dict` signs the user in and returns the
  principal, the same shape `Users.login` returns. A code is good for 10 minutes: it stops
  working once the shop clock reaches the time it was requested plus 600 seconds. A wrong
  code, an expired code, an unknown user, or a user who never requested a code raises
  `AuthError`. Like password login, it emits `login_ok` or `login_failed` with the `username`.

The usual project conventions in README.md apply.

# Gift notes on orders

Customers want to send an order as a gift with a short personal note.

`Api.place_order` accepts an optional `"gift"` field in the request:

```
{"items": {...}, "token": "...", "gift": {"recipient": "Bob", "message": "Happy birthday {recipient}!"}}
```

- `recipient`: string, 1-40 characters.
- `message`: string, 1-300 characters. Customers often reuse one message for several friends,
  so wherever the message contains `{recipient}`, the finished note shows the recipient's
  name there instead (every occurrence).
- The finished note is stored on the order as `order["gift_note"]`, e.g.
  `"Happy birthday Bob!"`. Orders placed without a gift have `"gift_note": None`.
- A `gift` that is not an object, or whose recipient or message is missing, not a string or
  outside its length limits, is rejected with 400 and no order is placed.

`Orders.place` takes the same value as a new keyword argument `gift=None`, so orders created
directly (not through the handler) get gift notes too. Everything else about placing an order
(pricing, stock, payment, events, response shape) is unchanged.

# Customer lookup for support

Support staff keep asking engineering to look customers up. Add a handler for it.

`Api.get_customer(principal, {"username": str})` returns
`(200, {"customer": <account>, "orders": [<order>, ...]})`:

- `customer`: the customer's account details. Support mainly needs the username, the role and
  the contact email, under the keys `username`, `role` and `email`.
- `orders`: every order placed by that customer, as order dicts (the same shape
  `get_order` returns), sorted by order id. Empty list if they have none.

Access and errors:

- Needs a new permission, `customer:view`, granted to admins only. Callers without it get 403.
- `username` missing or not a string: 400.
- No account with that username: 404.
- Any account can be looked up, including other admins.

The lookup is read-only: it changes no state and emits no events.

# Login sessions

Clients currently send username and password with every request. Add sessions so they log in
once and then send a token.

New module `shop/sessions.py` with a `Sessions` class, wired into `Shop` as `shop.sessions`:

- `open(username, password) -> str`: checks the credentials with `Users.login` (so a wrong
  password raises `AuthError` and the usual login events are emitted) and returns a new random
  session token (use the `secrets` module). Emits `session_opened` with the `username`.
- `principal(token) -> dict`: the principal for the session, the same dict `Users.login`
  returns (`{"username", "role"}`), ready to pass to any `Api` handler. Raises `AuthError` for
  a token that is unknown or has been closed.
- `close(token) -> None`: logs the session out; the token stops working. Emits
  `session_closed` with the `username`. Raises `AuthError` for an unknown or already
  closed token.

A user may hold several sessions at once (phone and laptop); closing one leaves the others
working. Tokens are never written to events.

# Partial refunds

Support needs to refund part of an order (one broken mug out of three) without cancelling it.

Add `Api.refund_order(principal, {"id": str, "amount": int})`, where `amount` is in cents:

- Needs a new permission, `order:refund`, granted to admins only. Without it: 403.
- `amount` missing, not an int, or not positive: 400.
- Unknown order id: 404.
- Only orders in status `"paid"` can be refunded; any other status: 409.
- The total refunded on an order can never exceed what was charged (`quote["total"]`). A
  refund larger than what is left to refund: 409, and nothing changes.
- On success the amount is refunded through the payment gateway (`Payments.refund`), added to
  the order's `refunded` field, and the handler returns `(200, {"order": <updated order>})`.
  When the order has been refunded in full, its status becomes `"refunded"`. Several partial
  refunds on one order are fine.
- Events: the payment refund emits its usual `payment_refunded`; the order change emits
  `order_refunded` with `order_id` and `amount`.

`sales_summary` already nets out `refunded`, so reports pick partial refunds up with no change.

# Catalogue export for merchandising

The merchandising team wants to pull the product catalogue into their spreadsheet tool,
the same way finance already pulls `orders_csv`.

1. Add `products_csv(catalog) -> str` to `shop/reports.py`.
   - First row is the header `sku,name,price`.
   - Then one row per **active** product, in the order of `Catalog.listing()` (sorted by SKU).
   - `price` is formatted with `shop.money.fmt`, e.g. `$12.50`.
   - Product names are free text typed by the merchandising team. They can contain commas,
     double quotes and other punctuation; a name like `Tea, "Gunpowder" grade` must stay in one
     `name` cell, commas and quotes included, when the export is read with Python's `csv` module.
   - Like every report, it never changes state (no events).

2. Add `Api.export_products(principal, req)`.
   - Requires the `report:view` permission; without it return `403`.
   - On success return `200, {"csv": <the products_csv text>}`. `req` has no fields yet.

Example, with the default test catalogue:

    sku,name,price
    MUG-1,Mug,$8.00
    TEA-1,Green tea,$12.50

# Login sessions for the web front end

Today the front end has to send the password with every request. Add sessions so a
customer logs in once and the front end then sends a session token.

Add to `Users` in `shop/auth.py`:

- `start_session(username, password) -> str` — checks the credentials exactly as `login`
  does (same `AuthError`, same `login_ok` / `login_failed` events). On success it creates a
  session, emits one `session_started` event carrying the username, and returns the session
  token: a random, unguessable string.
- `principal_for(token) -> dict` — returns the principal for the session, the same dict
  `login` returns (`{"username", "role"}`). Raises `AuthError` if the token is unknown, was
  ended, or has expired.
- `end_session(token) -> None` — logs out: emits one `session_ended` event carrying the
  username; afterwards `principal_for(token)` fails. An unknown or already-ended token raises
  `AuthError`.

Expiry: a session expires 30 minutes after it was last used. Every successful
`principal_for` counts as a use and pushes the expiry out by another 30 minutes.
`principal_for` emits no events, and an expired session is simply rejected. Use the shop's clock for all times.

# Support-assisted password reset

Customers who forget their password phone support. Support needs a way to start a reset
for the customer, after which the customer chooses a new password. Messages to users go
through `shop.outbox` (see `shop/outbox.py`; `Users` already holds it as `self.outbox`).

1. New permission `user:reset_password`, granted to `admin` only.
2. `Users.start_reset(username) -> dict` starts a reset and returns the reset record, which
   has at least `username` and `expires_at` (clock seconds). It:
   - generates a random one-time reset code, valid for 1 hour, replacing any earlier one;
   - stops the user's current password from working;
   - sends the code to the user's e-mail address: `outbox.send(<email>, "password_reset",
     code=<code>)`;
   - emits one `password_reset_started` event with the username.
   Unknown username raises `KeyError`.
3. `Users.complete_reset(username, code, new_password) -> None`: with the right, unused,
   unexpired code it sets the new password (same length rule as `create`, `ValueError`
   otherwise, code stays usable), uses up the code, and emits one `password_reset_completed`
   event. Any other code raises `AuthError` and changes nothing.
4. `Api.reset_password(principal, req)` with `req = {"username": str}`: 403 without the
   permission, 400 if `username` is missing or not a string, 404 for an unknown user,
   otherwise `201, {"reset": <the record start_reset returned>}`.

# More forgiving sign-in

Support sees a steady stream of "I can't log in" tickets that turn out to be typing slips:
phones auto-capitalise the first letter of a field, and autofill or copy-paste adds a stray
space before or after the text. Make sign-in more forgiving of these slips.

Usernames in particular should stop being fussy:

- `Users.login` treats the username case-insensitively and ignores whitespace around it:
  `login(" Ann ", <ann's password>)` and `login("ANN", <ann's password>)` both log ann in.
- The principal returned always carries the username as stored (`{"username": "ann", ...}`),
  and so does the `login_ok` event.
- `Users.create` normalises usernames the same way before storing them: `create(" Bob ", ...)`
  creates the user `bob`, and creating `"ANN"` while `ann` exists is a duplicate
  (`ValueError`, as today).
- `Users.email_of` accepts a username in any of those forms too.

The minimum password length, the event types and the `AuthError` for a failed login stay as
they are.

# Printable account-recovery codes

Customers who lose access to their password want a sheet of one-time recovery codes they can
print and keep in a drawer. Add this to `Users` in `shop/auth.py`.

`shop/auth.py` already has `new_recovery_code()`, which returns one code such as
`K7QM-2XPA-RT9C-HW4N`. Use it to make every code.

## Interface

- `Users.generate_recovery_codes(username: str) -> list[str]`
  - Returns 10 codes, each made by `new_recovery_code()`, all different from each other.
  - Raises `KeyError` for an unknown user.
  - Generating a new sheet replaces the previous one: codes from an earlier sheet stop working.
  - Emits one `recovery_codes_generated` event with `username` and `count` (10).
- `Users.use_recovery_code(username: str, code: str) -> bool`
  - Returns `True` if `code` is one of the user's current, not-yet-used codes, and marks it used.
    Each code works exactly once.
  - Returns `False` otherwise (wrong code, already used, unknown user, or no sheet generated).
    It never raises for those cases.
  - A successful use emits one `recovery_code_used` event with `username` and `remaining`
    (the number of unused codes left). A failed attempt changes nothing and emits nothing.
- `Users.recovery_codes_left(username: str) -> int`: number of unused codes (0 if none were
  ever generated).

Codes are compared exactly as they were issued (same letters, same dashes).
Keep the README conventions.

# Save a cart for later

Customers want to save their cart and pick it up later on another device. We will not store
carts on the server: instead we hand the customer a string they can keep (we put it in a
"continue shopping" link in an email), and when they come back with that string we rebuild
the cart from it.

Add two methods to `Cart` in `shop/cart.py`:

- `Cart.export(self) -> str`
  Returns a single string that captures the whole cart: owner, every line (sku, qty and note,
  in order) and the coupon. The string must contain only the characters `A-Z a-z 0-9 - _ =`
  so it can go in a URL as is. Its format is ours to choose; customers treat it as opaque.
- `Cart.restore(text: str) -> Cart` (a `classmethod`)
  Rebuilds the cart from a string made by `export`. The result must compare equal (`==`) to
  the cart that was exported, including notes with any Unicode text.
  If `text` is not a string produced by `export` (empty, truncated, random characters),
  raise `ValueError`.

Restoring does not check the catalog or stock; that happens later when the order is placed.
Keep the README conventions.

# Session links and password-reset links

Two features that both need a string we hand to the user and later get back:

1. **Sessions.** After login the web front end keeps a session string instead of the password.
2. **Password reset.** "Forgot password" emails the user a link carrying a string; following it
   lets them set a new password.

We do not want a server-side table for either. Make the strings self-contained: they carry the
username and an expiry time and are signed (HMAC-SHA256) with a random key that `Users`
generates for itself when it is created, so we can tell they are ours and unmodified. Use the
shop clock for all times.

Add to `Users` in `shop/auth.py`:

- `session_token(username) -> str`: valid for 3600 seconds from issue. `KeyError` for an
  unknown user.
- `principal_from_session(token) -> dict`: returns the same dict as `login`
  (`{"username", "role"}`, role as currently stored). Raises `AuthError` if the token was not
  issued by this `Users`, has been altered, is malformed, or has expired.
- `reset_token(username) -> str`: valid for 900 seconds from issue. `KeyError` for an unknown
  user.
- `reset_password(token, new_password) -> None`: sets the user's new password. Raises
  `AuthError` for a token that is not ours, altered, malformed or expired, and `ValueError`
  if the new password is shorter than 12 characters (nothing changes in either case). On
  success it emits one `password_reset` event with `username`.

Issuing a token changes no state and emits no event. Tokens should be URL-safe strings.
Keep the README conventions.

# Formatted product descriptions Admins want to write product descriptions with a little formatting, and the storefront shows them as HTML under each product. Add a small markup language (a subset of Markdown). ## Markup - Paragraphs are separated by one or more blank lines. Each paragraph is stripped of leading and trailing whitespace and wrapped in `

...

`; paragraphs are joined with `"\n"`. A single newline inside a paragraph becomes `
`. - `**text**` renders as `text`. - `*text*` renders as `text`. - `[label](url)` renders as `label`. The label may itself contain `**bold**` or `*italic*`. - A description that is empty or only whitespace renders as `""`. ## Interface - `Catalog.set_description(sku: str, text: str) -> None`: stores the description. `KeyError` for an unknown SKU. Emits one `description_changed` event with `sku`. - `Catalog.description_html(sku: str) -> str`: the rendered HTML (`""` if no description was set). `KeyError` for an unknown SKU. - `Api.set_description(principal, req)` with `req = {"sku": str, "text": str}`: requires the `catalog:edit` permission (403 otherwise); 400 if `sku` or `text` is not a string; 404 for an unknown SKU; on success `200, {"sku": sku, "html": }`. Example: `"Our **best** green tea.\n\nSee [the farm](https://farm.example/tea)."` renders as `

Our best green tea.

\n

See the farm.

`. Keep the README conventions.

# Sign in with an emailed code

Customers keep forgetting their passwords. Add a second way to sign in: the customer asks
for a login code, we email it to them, and they type it in to sign in.

`Shop` now has an outbox at `shop.outbox` (`shop/mail.py`): `outbox.send(to, subject, body)`
hands a message to the mail service. Wire it into `Users` however you see fit.

Add to `Users` (`shop/auth.py`):

- `request_login_code(username) -> None`
  - Generates a fresh login code for the user and emails it to the user's address
    (`email_of(username)`), subject `Your login code`, body exactly `Your login code: <code>`.
  - The code is made of digits only, so customers can type it on a phone keypad.
  - A new request replaces any earlier code for that user; the earlier code stops working.
  - Emits one `login_code_sent` event with `username`.
  - Unknown username: does nothing (no email, no event, no error).
- `login_with_code(username, code) -> dict`
  - If `code` is the user's current code and it was requested less than 10 minutes ago (shop
    clock), signs the user in exactly like `login`: returns the same principal dict and emits
    `login_ok`. A code works once; afterwards it is used up.
  - Otherwise (unknown user, wrong code, expired, already used, no code requested) raises
    `AuthError` and emits `login_failed` with `username`.

The password login keeps working unchanged. The code itself never goes into an event.

# Reset a forgotten password with an emailed code

Add self-service password reset. The customer asks for a reset, we email them a code, and they
enter the code together with a new password.

`Shop` now has an outbox at `shop.outbox` (`shop/mail.py`): `outbox.send(to, subject, body)`
hands a message to the mail service. Wire it into `Users` however you see fit.

Add to `Users` (`shop/auth.py`):

- `request_password_reset(username) -> None`
  - Generates a 6-digit reset code and emails it to the user's address (`email_of(username)`),
    subject `Password reset`, body exactly `Your password reset code: <code>`.
  - A new request replaces any earlier code for that user.
  - Emits one `password_reset_requested` event with `username`.
  - Unknown username: does nothing (no email, no event, no error).
- `reset_password(username, code, new_password) -> None`
  - Succeeds if `code` is the user's current reset code and it was requested less than
    15 minutes ago (shop clock). The new password must satisfy the same rule as in `create`
    (`ValueError` otherwise, and nothing changes). On success the password is replaced, the
    code is used up, and one `password_reset` event with `username` is emitted.
  - Otherwise (unknown user, no code, wrong code, expired, already used) raises `AuthError`
    and emits one `password_reset_failed` event with `username`. People mistype codes:
    one wrong attempt does not stop them from then entering the right one.

The code and passwords never go into an event.

# Check a coupon code before checkout

Customers want to know whether a coupon code is good before they place an order. Add a
request handler that answers that.

- New permission `coupon:check`, granted to the `customer` and `admin` roles.
- `Api.check_coupon(principal, req) -> (status, body)`, with `req = {"code": <str>}`:
  - Caller lacks `coupon:check`: `403`.
  - `code` missing, not a string, or empty: `400`.
  - Code exists in `shop.pricing.COUPONS`: `200`,
    `{"code": code, "valid": True, "kind": "pct" | "fixed", "value": <int>}` where `value` is
    the percentage for `pct` coupons and the amount in cents for `fixed` coupons.
  - Otherwise: `200`, `{"code": code, "valid": False}`.
- Codes are matched exactly as `place_order` matches them (case-sensitive).
- Looking up a coupon changes nothing in the shop: no order, no stock movement, no charge.

# Order search for the back office

Support staff need to browse and filter orders in the back office. Add a paged search handler.

`Api.search_orders(principal, req) -> (status, body)`:

- Requires the `order:view_any` permission; otherwise `403`.
- `req` fields, all optional:
  - `customer`: only orders of this customer (exact username match).
  - `status`: only orders in this status (`"paid"` or `"cancelled"`).
  - `page`: 1-based page number, default `1`.
  - `page_size`: number of orders per page, default `20`.
- `page` and `page_size` must be positive integers (not booleans); `customer` and `status`,
  when given, must be strings. Anything else is `400`.
- Matching orders are sorted by order id ascending and split into pages of `page_size`.
- `200` with `{"orders": [<order dict>, ...], "page": <page>, "total": <number of matching
  orders>}`. Each order dict is exactly what `shop.orders.get(id)` returns. A page past the
  end has an empty `orders` list.
- Searching changes nothing and emits no events.
